standard.title: Developing Inquiry Questions
standard.description: develop questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems, and contemporary civic issues
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems (AC9HS6S01). At Y7 the shift is from general HASS inquiry questions to discipline-specific civics questions grounded in understanding of political and legal systems.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop focused questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems and contemporary civic issues.

nodes.label: Characteristics of effective civic inquiry questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the characteristics of effective civic inquiry questions — those that are focused, investigable, and connected to genuine issues in political or legal systems.
nodes.minimum_width: Distinguish between a too-broad question (e.g. 'What is democracy?') and a focused inquiry question (e.g. 'How does Australia's federal system divide powers?') and explain what makes the second more useful for investigation.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the characteristics of effective civic inquiry questions: focused scope, investigable with available sources, connected to real issues in political or legal systems; practise identifying which questions are well-scoped vs too broad or too narrow.
wider: Evaluate a set of example inquiry questions against quality criteria, ranking and justifying which would lead to the most productive investigations
Compare civic inquiry questions with scientific or historical inquiry questions to understand what disciplinary thinking looks like in each context
Develop criteria for assessing the quality of an inquiry question and apply them to evaluate questions generated by others
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot distinguish productive from unproductive inquiry questions, the investigation phase (S02, S03) will be misdirected — either scope creep or investigation of trivially answerable questions. This is the phase-entry gate for civic inquiry work.

response_modes.reason: Understanding what makes an inquiry question 'good' is a meta-cognitive step — students need to reason about the question itself before they can use it as an investigation tool. Invest in the criteria explicitly.

success_criteria: Identify at least two characteristics of an effective civic inquiry question
Distinguish between a too-broad question and a focused, investigable question and explain the difference

nodes.label: Developing a key inquiry question
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a focused key inquiry question related to a specific political or legal system topic, and explain what the question is designed to investigate.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop one focused inquiry question related to Australia's political or legal system and explain what a student would need to investigate to answer it.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a key question for a specific investigation (e.g. 'What is the rule of law and how does it apply to Australia's legal system?' or 'How does Australia's federal system divide powers?'); explain the scope and purpose of the question; identify what kinds of sources would help answer it.
wider: Develop a sequence of sub-questions from a key inquiry question, mapping how they build toward a complete answer
Revise an inquiry question after initial research to sharpen its focus or correct a misunderstanding — practising question iteration
Generate inquiry questions from current media coverage of a civic issue, practising how contemporary events can sharpen investigation focus

response_modes.reason: Developing a good inquiry question requires iteration and practice — students who produce their first question rarely get it right. Allow time for revision and peer critique before committing to an investigation path.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Using current events as question generators (e.g. news stories about court decisions or government policy debates) gives students practice at the authentic form of the skill — identifying what is actually worth investigating in a real civic context rather than in an academic exercise.
success_criteria: Develop a focused inquiry question about Australia's political or legal system
Explain what the question is designed to investigate and identify what sources would be useful

nodes.label: Using current events to generate civic questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use current events to generate focused questions that apply to a wider civic investigation, connecting news events to the underlying political or legal concepts they illustrate.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a current news event related to a civic issue and develop one question that connects the event to a broader political or legal concept.
nodes.typical_width: Use current events to generate questions that apply to a wider investigation; for example, derive a question about freedom of expression protections from a news story about misinformation; explain how the current event illustrates an underlying civic issue.
wider: Track a developing news story over several days and generate a sequence of questions that evolve as new information emerges, practising the dynamic nature of inquiry
Compare how the same current event generates different inquiry questions depending on whether the investigator is using a democratic, legal, or social cohesion lens
Investigate an international civic issue and develop questions that allow comparison with Australian systems — practising cross-contextual civic inquiry

response_modes.reason: Different current events surface different types of civic questions — using varied events (court decisions, election campaigns, government announcements, protest actions) builds the range of question types students can generate.

success_criteria: Identify a current event related to a civic issue and develop a focused question connecting it to a broader civic concept
Explain what makes this question more useful for civic investigation than simply asking 'what happened'
